1⁄2 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
review:
"I moved to Wanaka to find my place in the world, my passion and direction. Just as Don Facundo found his calling refining the rum making process, I've found mine in hospitality making cocktails. Te Anaka is my Legacy cocktail and my interpretation of the place I now call home, Wanaka, inspired by both the produce around me and by the flavour profile of Bacardí Carta Blanca. Te Anaka is my way of sharing this beautiful place, my home, with the world and showing people everywhere that they too can create paradise and enjoy Wanaka."

We say: Reminiscent of a Honeysuckle Daiquiri with salty sherry notes. The rum, fino sherry, honey and lemon juice combine brilliantly, smoothed and made frothy with egg white.
history: New Zealand BACARDÍ LEGACY 2016 winning cocktail by James Crinson, LaLaLand Lounge Bar, Wanaka.

name: Lachlan's Antiscorbutic
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Rutte Celery Dry Gin
1⁄4 shot	Giffard Crème de Framboise
1⁄2 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1⁄12 shot	Pickle juice/brine/vinegar from pickled cucumber/gherkin
review: With its delicate shade of pink from a splash of raspberry liqueur, this cocktail is feistier than it appears with salty gherkin flavours combining brilliantly with celery gin.
history: Adapted from a recipe created in 2016 by Keli Rivers at Whitechapel Bar, San Francisco, USA. Keli presented this very tasty cocktail at a seminar on gin and genever at Tales of the Cocktail in July 2016, which is where we were lucky enough to first try it. Originally made with Rutte Celery Gin, the flavour of this gin contributes greatly to that of the finished cocktail.

name: Sweet Grape Caipirinha (Caipirinha D'uva)
garnish: Stirrer (spoon, wooden lolly stick or stick cut from sugar cane)
preparation:
1. Cut lime in half (from pole to pole) and then slice one of the halves into eight 3-4mm thick half-moon shaped segments and drop into the base of a robust rocks glass.

2. Add 3 bar spoons caster sugar (or ½oz / 15ml sugar syrup 2:1) and MUDDLE.

3. Add red grapes and MUDDLE some more.

4. When sure fruit juice is fully extracted and the sugar dissolved, transfer the muddled fruit and sugar into serving glass (preferably a 30cl / 10oz hi-ball glass).

5. POUR cachaça (stored in the freezer) and Sauternes into the rocks glass (used to muddle) and swirl to rinse glass before pouring cachaça into serving glass. STIR to ensure all ingredients are well mixed.

6. Crack (rather than crush) four to five large ice cubes using an Ice Tapper and drop into serving glass. STIR before topping with more ice and serve with a stirrer (but no straws).
ingredients:
1⁄2 fresh	Lime (fresh) (chopped)
3 barspoon	Caster/ Superfine/Baker's special sugar (white)
6 fresh	Red grapes (seedless)
3⁄4 shot	Sauternes dessert wine
2 shot	Cachaça (from freezer)
review: Flavours of grape, both fresh and in the wine, transform the humble Caipirinha into a Caipirinha D'uva.
history: For information on the history and other variations of the Caipirinha, please see our Caipirinha cocktail page.

name: Journey of Brothers
preparation: STIR first 4 ingredients with ice and strain into ice-filled glass. TOP with tonic water and briefly stir.
ingredients:
1 1⁄3 shot	Blended Scotch whisky
2⁄3 shot	Calvados / apple brandy / straight applejack
1⁄2 shot	Fino sherry
1 dash	Celery bitters
3 shot	Thomas Henry Tonic Water
review: Dry and lightly fruity with herbal minerality, this is a superbly refreshing and complex long drink.
history:
Adapted from a recipe created in 2018 by Alex Godfrey at Milk Thistle in Bristol, England.

Originally based on Chivas 12 Year Old Scotch with Somerset Cider cordial rather than calvados, this cocktail won the 2018 Chivas Masters Competition in London.

name: Jabberwock
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
1 shot	Fino sherry
1⁄2 shot	Blanc quinquina/kina (e.g. Mattei Cap Corse or Kina L'Aéro d'Or)
1⁄2 shot	Lillet Blanc (or other aromatized wine)
2 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
review: Mouth-puckeringly dry, this is a great aperitivo with quinine, fino sherry, gin botanicals and citrus all singing harmoniously.
history: Named after Lewis Carroll's Jabberwoky poem, this recipe is adapted from one in Harry Craddock's 1930 The Savoy Cocktail Book which calls for a now defunct product called Caperitif. A notation accompanies Craddock's recipe, "This will made you gyre and gimble in the wabe until brillig all right, all right." Proving that be was a Lewis Carroll fan.

name: Sunray
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
2⁄3 shot	Bourbon whiskey
2⁄3 shot	Grand Marnier or other cognac orange liqueur
1⁄3 shot	Lillet Blanc (or other aromatized wine)
1⁄3 shot	Blanc quinquina/kina (e.g. Mattei Cap Corse or Kina L'Aéro d'Or)
3⁄4 shot	Orange juice (freshly squeezed)
review: Citrusy, bourbon-laced and gently bittersweet with fresh zippy rich orange.
history: First published in William James "Billy" Tarling's 1937 Café Royal Bar Book where the invention of this cocktail is credited to "A. L. Jones." The Sunray was brought to our attention by Jason E. Clapham of St. Edward's MCR at Oxford, England who recommends making it with Cocchi Americano in place of the Kina Lillet used in the 1937 recipe.

name: Psychopathia Sexualis
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1⁄2 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
1⁄2 shot	Palo cortado sherry
1⁄2 shot	Strucchi Dry Vermouth
1⁄2 shot	Strucchi Rosso Vermouth
1 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
review: Your choice of sherry greatly affects the finished cocktail I we ummm'd and ahhhh'd between dry oloroso, palo cortado, and amontillado sherries before settling on the slightly richer palo cortado, but any of these sherries produce a delicious cocktail.
history:
Recipe adapted from Grosby Gaige's 1941 Cocktail Guide And Ladies' Companion with instructs, "Shake well with cracked ice and strain into cocktail glass. Sadly, Gaige doesn't stipulate what kind of sherry, merely stipulating "¼ part Sherry."

This cocktail takes its name from Richard Freiheer von Krafft-Ebing's 1886 book Psychopathia Sexualis (Psychopathy of Sex). This controversial German book "deals with the psychology of deviant sexual behaviour" and is noted for being the first to use the terms sadism and masochism.

name: Hunter's Verdict
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into ice-filled glass (preferably over a chunk of block ice).
ingredients:
2 shot	Caribbean blended rum aged 6-10 years
3⁄4 shot	Amaro (e.g. Montenegro)
1⁄4 shot	Ginger liqueur
1 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
1 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
review: Brilliantly balanced and composed, this is a rum-forward boozy digestive with herbal complexity and enlivening ginger to contemplate a great meal and a good yarn relayed by a fellow diner.
history:
Adapted from a 2020 recipe by Jason E. Clapham, Oxford, England, which specifies 60ml Plantation Xaymaca Jamaican rum, 22.5ml Amaro Montenegro and 7.5ml King's Ginger.

Jason explains, "Hunter's Verdict, where big Jamaican flavours are melded with King's Ginger and Amaro Montenegro (incidentally, the name refers to Dr John Hunter, who declared Jamaica rum safe to drink in 1788 – the lead pipes were to blame! - and henceforth Jamaican rum would feature prominently in Navy rations)."

name: Coco Geisha
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Japanese single malt whisky
3⁄4 shot	Akashi-Tai Daiginjo Genshu sake (chilled)
3⁄4 shot	Coconut water (chilled)
1⁄4 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
review: Delicately enriched whisky, sake and coco water – a trio that sits together harmoniously.
history: Created in February 2021 by yours truly at the Clocktower, Rye, England.

name: Fix One's Flint
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1⁄2 shot	Horse with No Name habanero bourbon
2 shot	Lillet Blanc (or other aromatized wine)
1 shot	Oloroso sherry
1 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
2 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: While the name may suggest aggression this aperitivo is gentle, caressing, and only moderately flinted in alcohol.
history: To "fix one's flint" means to settle a matter in Cowboy speak so, appropriately, this is a riff on Sean Frederick's Flintlock cocktail (by yours truly in September 2021).

name: Triumph of Pompeii
preparation: SHAKE first 4 ingredients with ice and strain into ice-filled glass. TOP with soda.
ingredients:
1 1⁄4 shot	Americano bianco
3⁄4 shot	Fernet Branca liqueur
1 shot	Pink grapefruit juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄3 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 shot	Thomas Henry Pink Grapefruit soda
review: Top with soda and immediately serve/enjoy. Experiencing this cocktail's light fluffy foamy entry to its bittersweet, earthy, almost coal dust and liquorice herbal depths is so good you'll want a fresh one to suck the foam off of. A triumph!
history: Adapted from a recipe created in 2012 by Tyler Wang at No. 9 Park, in Boston, USA. Apparently inspired by Milk & Honey's Rome is Burning cocktail. I've used pink grapefruit soda as I believe this adds to this cocktail more than the club soda called for in Tyler's original recipe.

name: Dot (by Jason Clapham)
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
1 shot	Fino sherry
1⁄2 shot	De Kuyper Apricot Brandy liqueur
1⁄3 shot	White overproof rum
1⁄4 shot	Chilled water (optional)
review: I've cut the overproof rum by a third from the original recipe to allow the other ingredients space to shine in this delicious Martini-like, dry and spirituous aperitivo.
history: Adapted from a recipe by Jason E. Clapham at the St. Edward's MCR at Oxford, England and inspired by the Dot cocktail in the 1937 The Café Royal Cocktail Book. Jason says, "This one came about as a fortuitous misreading: I read Curaçao as Cachaça, and then subbed overproof rum. The original is a far more straightforward affair, though more than pleasant." Jason's original recipe: 30 ml dry gin, 30 ml fino sherry, 15 ml Wray & Nephew overproof white rum, and 15 ml apricot liqueur.

name: Boothby Cocktail
preparation: STIR first 4 ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass. TOP with sparkling wine.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Straight rye whiskey (100 proof /50% alc./vol.)
5⁄6 shot	Strucchi Rosso Vermouth
1 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
2 drop	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
5⁄6 shot	Brut champagne/sparkling wine (chilled)
review: "A delectable Manhattan, with a sparkling wine float."
history:
Named after The Honorable William T. "Cocktail Bill" Boothby (1862-1930), bartender, cocktail book author, prosecuted speakeasy operator, and California Congressman. Boothby is believed to have created his namesake cocktail around the turn of the 20th century while bar manager of the Pied Piper Bar in the Palace Hotel, San Fransico, as corroborated in the Santa Cruz Evening News on the 8th August 1930 [see below].

Surprisingly, the Boothby Cocktail doesn't appear in any of the numerous books he penned during his lifetime, other than a verse in his 1908 The World's Drinks and How to Mix Them.

name: Medium Dry Martini
garnish: Grapefruit zest twist (expressed & discarded) & skewered olive
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
2 1⁄2 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
1⁄4 shot	Strucchi Bianco Vermouth
1⁄6 shot	Ambrato/ambre/amber vermouth
1⁄12 shot	Fino sherry
1 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
review: My preferred five-to-one Dry Martini ratio, but with the fortified wine split between dry vermouth, bianco vermouth and fino sherry.
history: Created in April 2023 by yours truly at The Clocktower, Rye, England.

name: Chauncey
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
3⁄4 shot	Hayman's Old Tom Gin
3⁄4 shot	Straight rye whiskey (100 proof /50% alc./vol.)
3⁄4 shot	Strucchi Rosso Vermouth
3⁄4 shot	Cognac (brandy)
1 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
review: A delicious, spilt base, equal parts, Sweet Manhattan-style cocktail suited to late-night sipping.
history: A pre-Prohibition cocktail from the Big Brass Rail bar of the original Waldorf Astoria Hotel in New York City, USA. The Chauncey first appears in Albert Stevens Crockett's 1931 Old Waldorf Astoria Bar Days.

name: Rhum Marianito
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into ice-filled glass (preferably over a large cube or chunk of block ice).
ingredients:
2 1⁄2 shot	Strucchi Rosso Vermouth
1⁄2 shot	Rhum Clément Blanc
1⁄2 shot	Orange Curaçao liqueur
3 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
2 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: An agricole rhum-laced riff on the traditional Spanish Marianito.
history: Adapted from a recipe created in 2004 by Nialls Fallon at his Eel Bar in Manhattan, New York City, USA. Originally made with Atxa Rojo vermouth and Holmes Cay rhum agricole.

name: Air Mail
garnish: Tip of a mint sprig or serve naked
preparation: SHAKE first 3 ingredients with ice and strain into an ice-filled glass (preferably a column of ice). TOP with sparkling wine.
ingredients:
1 shot	Light gold rum (1-3 year old molasses column)
1⁄2 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄2 shot	Honey syrup (3 honey to 1 water)
1 1⁄2 shot	Brut champagne/sparkling wine
review:
Lightly or well-aged rum invigorated with dry champagne, freshened by a touch of lime and balanced by honeyed richness.

Described by some as being a rum-based French 75, like the French 75, there is debate over the correct glass and whether to serve with ice. The truth: the Air Mail is best as it was originally intended, served as a highball in a highball glass (max capacity 10oz / 300ml).
history:
This is a potent little drink and the name could be a reference to airmail being the quickest way of getting a letter from A to B. It could date back to the early days of airmail which began 15th May 1918 with the world's first scheduled airmail route between New York and Washington D.C.. However, the earliest known reference to the drink is a 1930s promotional pamphlet, Bacardi and Its Many Uses.

The Air Mail (spelled with two words) most notably appears in W.C. Whitfield's 1941 wooden cover bound Here's How accompanied by the note "It ought to make you fly high." Indeed, the 1940s appear to be the Air Mail's heyday with the drink notably also appearing in David Embury's 1948 The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks and Esquire's 1949 Handbook for Hosts.

That Bacardi leaflet calls for Bacardi Gold rum while Whitfield specifies "fine rum" [well-aged blended Caribbean rums work well]. Both recipes stipulate a highball glass [a tall glass smaller than 10oz / 295ml] filled with ice. This is a "short drink served long" and misguided folk who serve it straight-up in a coupe or flute are taking a flight of fancy.

name: Silk Stocking
garnish: Dust with freshly grated nutmeg (or cinnamon powder)
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
2 shot	Patrón Silver blanco tequila
3⁄4 shot	Dutch Cacao white crème de cacao
1⁄4 shot	Giffard Grenadine syrup
3⁄4 shot	Single cream/half-and-half
review: So smooooooth but still retains a tequila bite and a hint of chocolate and fruit.
history:
This recipe is from Ryan Chetiyawardana in 2009, who shared his recipe at The Cabinet Room, London during the UK finals of that year's World Class bartending competition.

The Silk Stocking originated in the late 1970s - early 1980s, and the earliest cocktail book I've seen it referenced is as a blended cocktail in Helen Spence's 1982 book Cocktails For Two.

name: The Slope
garnish: Dried apricot on rim or skewered Luxardo Maraschino cherry
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
2 shot	Straight rye whiskey (100 proof /50% alc./vol.)
2⁄3 shot	Punt E Mes vermouth amaro
1⁄3 shot	De Kuyper Apricot Brandy liqueur
1 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
review: Stirred and spirit-forward and Manhattan / Brooklyn-like. Rye whiskey-based with aromatised wine complexity and apricot brandy adding flavoursome fruity richness. A delightful late-night sipper.
history:
Named after the Park Slope area of Brooklyn in New York City, this cocktail was created in 2009 by Julie Reiner as the House Manhattan for the opening menu of her bar Clover Club, which sits a couple of neighbourhoods away from Park Slope in Brooklyn's Carrol Gardens.

Our 6:2:1 formula is courtesy of G. M. Genovese, a fellow Discerning Drinker, in November 2023. The original spec called for a whopping 75ml (1½oz rye whiskey, 22.5ml (¾oz) Punt E Mes, 10ml (⅓oz) apricot brandy, and 1 dash aromatic bitters.

name: Manhattan Transfer

Adapted from a recipe created in 2013 by Phil Ward at Mayahuel in New York City, USA.

name: Farmer's Tan

review: Mezcal, vermouth amaro and orange curaçao combine is a spirit-forward spipper.
history: Created in 2016 by Seth Brammer at Filament, Dallas, Texas, USA. (Seth's original recipe calls for Wahaka Reposado con Gusano Mezcal and Ferand Dry Curaçao).

name: Mexican in Manhattan
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
2 shot	Patrón Añejo tequila
1⁄12 shot	Luxardo Maraschino liqueur
1 shot	Strucchi Bianco Vermouth

review: I tried making my usual Sweet Manhattan but with añejo tequila as the base spirit and it was not half bad, but there's something about tequila that says 'white' rather than 'red' vermouth. I also started with my favourite addition to a Sweet Manhattan: a half spoon of syrup from the maraschino cherry jar, but añejo tequila is so much more suited to maraschino liqueur. So I switched sweet vermouth for bianco vermouth and Angostura Bitters for lavender bitters. (I love the combination of tequila and lavender.) Hope you like the result.
history:
Created 25th January 2017 by yours truly at the Cabinet Room, London, England.

Adapted from a recipe created in 2017 by Philip Bischoff at Manhattan Bar, Singapore.

1⁄4 shot	Disaronno amaretto
1⁄4 shot	Difford's Falernum liqueur

name: Los Pacaminos Margarita

1⁄4 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)

5 drop	Difford's Margarita Bitters
review: A mellow but characterful Margarita distinguished by a splash of corn whisky, mezcal and corn liqueur, further mellowed by agave syrup and a split between lemon and lime.
history: Created in February 2023 by yours truly for both Margarita Day and to celebrate Paul Young's Los Pacaminos Tex-Mex band playing at the local village hall a few days later. There are 10 ingredients - there's a lot of members of the band.

name: French 75 (Difford's recipe)
preparation: STIR powdered sugar with lemon juice in base of shaker until sugar dissolves. Add next 5 ingredients (all but champagne), SHAKE with ice and strain into ice-filled glass. TOP with champagne and lightly stir. (Consider pouring half the champagne into the glass first to help reduce foaming and eliminate need to stir.)
ingredients:
1 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
2 barspoon	Powdered sugar (white sugar ground in mortar and pestle) (or use 5ml of 2:1 sugar syrup per spoon)
1⁄2 shot	Hayman's Old Tom Gin
1⁄2 shot	Calvados / apple brandy / straight applejack
1⁄2 shot	Cognac (brandy)
1⁄6 shot	Giffard Grenadine syrup
2 dash	La Fée Parisienne absinthe
2 1⁄2 shot	Brut champagne/sparkling wine
review:
I've Colin Field to thank for my French 75 epiphany. One evening in early June 2017 I was sat at his bar (Bar Hemingway) and he showed me the vintage 75ml gun cartridge he keeps there and pointed out how it is shaped like a tall Collins glass and not a flute. The French 75 was originally served in a tall cartridge-shaped glass, and I now agree with Colin – it is a drink that should pack a punch and should be served in a Collins glass. I'm now also the proud owner of two vintage 75mm cartridges, one being a fine example of trench art.

So, there you have it; it took a man called Colin to persuade me to use a Collins glass. Incidentally, Colin's bar lies a 5-minute walk away from where the '75' Cocktail is thought to have been created.
history:
Created by yours truly, this combines Robert Vermeire's 1922 French 75 with the cognac and champagne now so identified with this classic. And thanks to Colin Field's influence, this French 75 is served in an ice-filled Collins glass rather than straight-up in a flute or coupe.
See: French 75 history.

Adapted from numerous other Bamboo recipes by yours truly on 2nd August 2014 and further 'perfected' in January 2023.

name: El Presidente
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Light gold rum (1-3 year old molasses column)
1 shot	Strucchi Dry Vermouth
1⁄3 shot	Orange Curaçao liqueur
1⁄12 shot	Giffard Grenadine syrup
2 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review:
Rum and vermouth combine harmoniously in this delicate and subtly citrus-fresh cocktail.

My previous El Presidente version involved the use of three different vermouths:
- 45ml (1½oz) Gold lightly aged light rum
- 20ml (⅔oz) Dry vermouth
- 15ml (½oz) Bianco vermouth
- 10ml (⅓oz) Orange Curaçao liqueur
- 5ml (⅙oz) Rosso (sweet) vermouth
- 2.5ml (1⁄12oz) Grenadine (pomegranate) syrup
- 4 drops Difford's Daiquiri Bitters (optional)
history:
My (yours truly) version of an El Presidente combines elements of its many variations over the decades.

Thought to have been created in the mid-1910s in Havana, Cuba. In his 2015 Imbibe! Updated and Revised, David Wondrich credits the creation of what he calls the "Cubanized answer to the Manhattan" to Constantino Ribalaigua while "the head bartender at a little café just off the Parque Central in Havana." Wondrich says, "Constante's claim is found in a 1937 article by Jack Cuddy, who interviewed him while he was in Havana."

The earliest known recipe for a Presidente was discovered in Cuba's Biblioteca Nacional by French historian Fernando Castellon in a book called Manual del Cantinero by John B. Escalante published in Havana in 1915. The fact that the Presidente was a popular drink in Cuba by the late 1910s is supported by a 1919 article from the New York Evening Standard, which declares the Presidente a "favourite drink of the Cubans". And, on page 40 of his 1928 book When it's cocktail time in Cuba, Basil Woon says of this drink, "It is the aristocrat of cocktails and is the one preferred by the better class of Cuban".

Many modern-day recipes for a Presidente include a splash of lime juice, but this is not found in the 1915 Manual del Cantinero or other vintage recipes where vermouth counters rich grenadine. Indeed, in his 1948 The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks, David Embury (writing about the Daiquiri) explains, "If vermouth instead of citrus is used with the grenadine, the name is El Presidente." He then directs readers to page 158, where he says, "The leading rum cocktail of the aromatic type is El Presidente. Gold label rum is somewhat more pleasing than white label when combined with vermouth and is therefore used in this and many other aromatic type cocktails". Embury adds,"This recipe may be varied by adding 1 or 2 dashes of curaçao to each drink" and a few drops of curaçao is the first ingredient in the Manuel del Cantinero recipe (which Wondrich translates from the Spanish original in Imbibe!).

name: Dantes in Fernet
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 shot	Speyburn 10yo Speyside single malt
1⁄6 shot	Fernet Branca liqueur
1 shot	Blood orange juice
1⁄3 shot	Maple syrup
1 dash	Xocolatl mole bitters
review: It's obvious that this Blood & Sand-like cocktail contains Fernet, it has an almost smoky herbal influence. Maple syrup is an inspired sweetener and flavour enhancer.
history: Adapted from a recipe created in September 2013 by Mickaël Lenu, a Frenchman while working at Ancestral bar in Wellington, New Zealand.

name: Perfect Summit Manhattan
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
ingredients:
2 1⁄2 shot	Bourbon whiskey
3⁄4 shot	Strucchi Dry Vermouth
3⁄4 shot	Muscat (Rutherglen) wine
1⁄6 shot	Orange Curaçao liqueur
2 dash	Whiskey barrel-aged bitters
review: A riff on a Dry Manhattan given extra depth by the addition of dessert wine and whiskey bitters.
history:
Adapted from a recipe created by Pilar Zeglin at Summit Restaurant Bar in Cincinnati, USA, courtesy of Ardent Spirits.
See: Manhattan cocktail history

name: Simon Says
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Rutte Old Simon Genever
1⁄2 shot	Gentian liqueur (e.g. Suze, Salers etc)
1⁄6 shot	Galliano L'Autentico liqueur
1⁄6 shot	Bigallet Genepi Grand Tetras
1⁄6 shot	Dutch Cacao white crème de cacao
review: A great aperitif drink which uses bready genever and gentian liqueur as its backbone with spoons of herbal Galliano, genepi and chocolate liqueurs adding interest and complexity. (Be sure to use Galliano L'Authentico – not Galliano Vanilla.)
history: Created in 2016 by Joaquín Simó at Pouring Ribbons, New York City, USA, based on and named after Rutte's Old Simon genever.

name: Thimisis
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Bacardi Carta Blanca Superior White Rum
1⁄2 shot	Bigallet Thym
1⁄2 shot	Honey water (1:1)
2⁄3 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
2 dash	Bob's Lavender Bitters
review:
"As senses are the best way to recall a memory, I wanted to create a cocktail that can please our senses and help us remember the place where the Bacardi family began their journey: the Mediterranean. Thimisis clearly has a Mediterranean character and its name is both the Greek word for memory and the first letters of thyme. The reason thyme is so important is that in Ancient Greece it was a symbol of durability and resistance, two things that completely represent the Bacardi family."

We say: It took us a while to find our bottle of Bigallet Thyme liqueur but once we tried this drink we discovered it was worth searching out. This is basically a thyme and lavender daiquiri and it likes plenty of dilution. We found a floral honey worked best.
history: Greek BACARDÍ LEGACY 2016 winning cocktail by Konstantinos Kapniaris, Third Wave, Thessaloniki.

name: Tequila Alexander
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain back into shaker. DRY SHAKE (without ice) and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Patrón Añejo tequila
1⁄2 shot	De Kuyper Brown Crème de Cacao
1⁄2 shot	Dutch Cacao white crème de cacao
3⁄4 shot	Single cream/half-and-half
1⁄3 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
review: Creamy tequila and chocolate this tequila based riff on the classic Brandy Alexander is deliciously indulgent.
history:
Created in February 2017 by yours truly at the Cabinet Room in London, England.
Alexander cocktail history

name: 21st Century (Difford's recipe)
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Patrón Reposado tequila
5⁄6 shot	Dutch Cacao white crème de cacao
2⁄3 shot	Lillet Blanc (or other aromatized wine)
1⁄6 shot	Blanc quinquina/kina (e.g. Mattei Cap Corse or Kina L'Aéro d'Or)
1⁄6 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
review:
I revisited this cocktail in December 2022 when Jim Meehan made me aware of his, original 21st Century and I changed from Joerg Meyer's 20th Century spec to a recipe based on my favoured Twentieth Century (but with tequila as the base), the key difference being the aromatised wine used. For the record, the previous recipe on this page (without "Difford's recipe" in the title) comprised:
50 ml Reposado tequila
30 ml White crème de cacao
30 ml Cocchi Americano Bianco
10 ml Lemon juice

I also retested my preference for reposado rather than blanco tequila but I still favour the rounding effect of reposado in this cocktail.
history: I discovered the 21st Century, a tequila-based 20th Century Cocktail during Lockdown, in time for the 16th edition of our book. Regrettably, I didn't record where online I found it but it was only in December 2022 when I learnt, from the creator himself, that Jim Meehan created the tequila-based 21st Century Cocktail back in 2007 during his tenure at Manhattan's famous Pegu Club. A time before tequila's rise in popularity and before aromatised wines such as Cocchi Americano were imported into the USA.

name: Coronation G & Tea
garnish: Something British such as skewered honey comb, Scottish shortbread rested across rim or mini Cornish scone
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Beefeater Crown Jewel Gin
1⁄2 shot	Fino sherry
1⁄2 shot	Pineapple juice
1⁄2 shot	Chai tea (cold)
1⁄2 shot	Honey syrup (3 honey to 1 water)
review: Beefeater Crown Jewel, a suitably regal 50% alcohol-by-volume gin, provides the flavoursome backbone to this honeyed pineapple and Chia tea-flavoured cocktail with bone-dry fino sherry balancing the rich honey and contributing vinous complexity.
history: Created in April 2023, to celebrate the coronation of Charles III, by yours truly at The Clocktower, Rye, England.

name: Portobello Star Manhattan (Perfect)
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
2 shot	Straight rye whiskey (100 proof /50% alc./vol.)
1⁄2 shot	Strucchi Dry Vermouth
1⁄2 shot	Carpano Antica Formula Vermouth
12 drop	Bob's Abbotts bitters
review: Rye based (originally Jim Beam) perfectly served with dry vermouth and Antica Formula
history:
Jake Burger introduced his take on the Perfect Manhattan at the Portobello Star, Notting Hill, London, England in 2011 after working with Robert Petrie of Bob's Bitters fame to make a reproduction of Abbott's Bitters. Jake uses Jim Beam rye whiskey, Noilly Prat Blanc Original dry vermouth, Carpano Antica Formula and Abbott's Bitters.
Manhattan cocktail history

name: Raisin' Cane
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
2 shot	Pineau des Charentes rouge
1⁄2 shot	Martinique V.S.O.P rum
1⁄2 shot	Amontillado sherry
1 dash	Xocolatl mole bitters
review: Adapted from a recipe created by Myles Worrell at The Esquire Tavern in San Antonio, USA. Myles' original recipe called for 2oz Pineau des Charentes rouge, ½oz Paranubes Oaxacan rum, ½oz amontillado sherry and 1 dash Xocolatl Mole bitters.
history: Rich and yet balanced with the combination of sherry and red pineau des charentes contributing the eponymous raisin with rhum agricole adding distinctive grassy sugar "cane" notes.

name: Tokyo Drift
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
2 shot	Japanese blended whisky
3⁄4 shot	Strucchi Rosso Vermouth
1⁄2 shot	Light vermouth amaro (e.g. Cardamaro)
1⁄6 shot	Strega liqueur
review: Boozy yet delicate, beautifully balanced and complex. This Japanese whisky riff on a classic Manhattan benefits from freshening aniseed and minty notes from Strega.
history: Adapted from a recipe by Brad Farran, Raleigh, North Carolina, USA. Brad's original recipe calls for Yamazaki 12 year old. He named his cocktail in reference to the third instalment of the Fast and the Furious movies, which he thinks, "is pretty hilarious."

name: Bloody Mary (Difford's recipe)
garnish: Celery salt & black pepper rim + garnish with celery stick, cherry tomato & strip yellow bell pepper
preparation: MUDDLE pepper in base of shaker. Add other ingredients and ice then ROLL (rotate rather than shake shaker) and fine strain into ice-filled glass. Use ice fresh from freezer (rather than ice-machine/ice-well) to fill glass so avoid unwanted dilution.
ingredients:
1⁄2 ring	Yellow bell pepper (optional)
1 1⁄2 shot	Ketel One Vodka
2 1⁄4 shot	Tomato juice
1⁄3 shot	Amontillado sherry
1⁄3 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 pinch	Celery salt
3 grind	Black pepper
8 drop	Hot pepper sauce (red)
4 dash	Worcestershire sauce
review: A Bloody Mary Cocktail with a hint of bell pepper freshness and a touch of sherry.
history:
Created in 2007 by yours truly at the Cabinet Room, London, England.
Bloody Mary history

name: Obligatory Brooklyn
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Tennessee whiskey
1⁄2 shot	Carpano Antica Formula Vermouth
1⁄2 shot	Ambrato/ambre/amber vermouth
1⁄3 shot	Amaro Nonino Quintessentia
1⁄4 shot	Luxardo Maraschino liqueur
1⁄6 shot	Clementi China Antico Elixir
1⁄6 shot	Chilled water
review: Rich and slightly sweet but dried and balanced by herbal bitterness, perhaps the ultimate digestivo.
history: A riff on a classic Brooklyn cocktail created by Alex White and shared (in January 2021) via a comment on our Perfect Brooklyn page. Alex's original, very delicious, recipe calls for 7.5ml Luxardo Perla Dry in place of the easier to obtain maraschino liqueur I've used.

name: De Beauvoir
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 shot	Straight rye whiskey (100 proof /50% alc./vol.)
2⁄3 shot	Hazelnut liqueur
1⁄2 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1 3⁄4 shot	Smoked porter beer
1 barspoon	Demerara / dark Muscovado / brown sugar
1 dash	Whiskey barrel-aged bitters
review: Richly flavoured and lusciously bittersweet with rye whiskey, bitter porter and sour lemon juice balancing hazelnut liqueur and brown sugar.
history:
Created in 2013 by Andrea Montague from London, England to win the Difford's Guide Beer-tail Competition for London Cocktail Week 2013 held on Friday 9th August 2013 at our own Cabinet Room in London.

Named after De Beauvoir Town, an area of north London boundaried by Kingsland Road to the east, Southgate Road to the west, the Regent's Canal in the south and Tottenham Road to the north. The cockney name for the area, Beavertown, is also the name of the brewery in Hackney whose Smog Rocket porter Andrea used in her winning cocktail.

name: Cachaça Fruit Cup (Difford's Cup No.10)
garnish: Lemon, orange & strawberry slices, mint sprig & borage
preparation: POUR all ingredients into glass. Half fill glass with ice. Add a citrus slice and a couple of mint leaves from garnish before filling to brim with ice. Finish with rest of garnish.
ingredients:
5⁄6 shot	Cachaça
5⁄6 shot	Orange Curaçao liqueur
5⁄6 shot	Strucchi Rosso Vermouth
2 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
1 2⁄3 shot	Thomas Henry Ginger Ale
1 2⁄3 shot	Cola (e.g. Coca Cola or Pepsi Cola)
review: A fruit cup is just not as fruity when made with any other spirit – yes cachaça is distilled from fermented sugar cane juice rather than fruit, but in this cocktail it seems to amplify fruity and sweet notes. While it may not go down well at Wimbledon, we're sure it would be a hit in Rio.
history: Created in June 2017 by yours truly at the Cabinet Room, London, England. For more recipes and history see Fruit Cups and Pimm's.

name: Aged Rum Fruit Cup (Difford's Cup No.14)
garnish: Lemon, orange & strawberry slices, mint sprig & borage
preparation: POUR all ingredients into glass. Half fill glass with ice. Add a citrus slice and a couple of mint leaves from garnish before filling to brim with ice. Finish with rest of garnish.
ingredients:
5⁄6 shot	Caribbean blended rum aged 6-10 years
5⁄6 shot	Orange Curaçao liqueur
5⁄6 shot	Strucchi Rosso Vermouth
2 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
1 2⁄3 shot	Thomas Henry Ginger Ale
1 2⁄3 shot	Cola (e.g. Coca Cola or Pepsi Cola)
review: Aged rum's sweet notes add a richness to this flavoursome fruit punch, seemingly adding tropical fruitiness.
history: Created in June 2017 by yours truly at the Cabinet Room, London, England. For more recipes and history see Fruit Cups and Pimm's.

name: Tennessee Whiskey Fruit Cup (Difford's Cup No.17)
garnish: Lemon, orange & strawberry slices, mint sprig & borage
preparation: POUR all ingredients into glass. Half fill glass with ice. Add a citrus slice and a couple of mint leaves from garnish before filling to brim with ice. Finish with rest of garnish.
ingredients:
1 shot	Tennessee whiskey
5⁄6 shot	Orange Curaçao liqueur
5⁄6 shot	Strucchi Rosso Vermouth
2 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
1 2⁄3 shot	Thomas Henry Ginger Ale
1 2⁄3 shot	Cola (e.g. Coca Cola or Pepsi Cola)
review: Arguably, when numbering my fruit cups, I left the best till last. (I skipped number 16 because the number 7 so befits a Tennessee whiskey-based cocktail). If using a 40% alc./vol. Tennessee whiskey (as opposed to a higher alc./vol. special bottling) then this recipe benefits from an extra splash (5ml (1/6oz) to 10ml (1/3oz). Tennessee whiskey adds an appealing sweet toasty note to this fruit cup.
history: Created in June 2017 by yours truly at the Cabinet Room, London, England. For more recipes and history see Fruit Cups and Pimm's.

name: Palo Negro
preparation: STIR all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Patrón Reposado tequila
3⁄4 shot	Palo cortado sherry
1⁄3 shot	Dark/black/blackstrap rum
1⁄6 shot	Grand Marnier or other cognac orange liqueur
1⁄12 shot	Demerara/Muscovado/brown sugar syrup (2 sugar:1 water)
review: Tequila, rum, sherry and orange liqueur combine harmoniously in this complex spirit-led, after-dinner/late-night sipper.
history: Adapted from a recipe created by Ivy Mix at Leyenda, Brooklyn, New York City, USA. Incidentally, Palo Negro translates from Spanish as Black Stick.

name: Navy Grog
garnish: Ice cone with straw running through the centre, lime wedge, mints sprigs bouquet and flag
preparation:
BLEND all ingredients with 6oz scoop of crushed ice and pour into chilled glass. [If using xanthan gum, DRY BLEND (without ice first, then add crushed ice and blend again.]

How to make an Ice Cone: Ideally, use Beachbum Berry's Navy Grog Cone Kit to make your ice cones. This has a perfectly sized stainless steel cone mould and rod to make a hole for a thin sip straw. I use Berry's cone mould with a long stainless steel drinking straw instead of the supplied rod. Alternatively, use a pilsner glass as your ice cone mould.
1. Stand a metal straw/rod/ chopstick in the centre of your cone mould. This will form the hole through which the straw will run.
2. While holding the rod in place, pack the cone with finely shaved ice (snow ice). NOTE: Crushed ice is not fine enough.
3. Place in a freezer for at least an hour, ideally overnight.
4. Remove from freezer and leave to stand for a few minutes, then gently remove the rod and ice from the cone mould.
5. If ready to serve your cocktail, place the ice cone in the serving glass with a straw inserted through the central hole. Or, wrap the ice cone in plastic and return it to the freezer for storage, ideally within a sealed plastic box to prevent contamination from odours.
ingredients:
1 shot	Light white rum (charcoal-filtered 1-4 years old)
1 shot	Caribbean blended rum aged 6-10 years
1 shot	Navy rum (54.5% alc./vol.)
1⁄4 shot	Pimento dram/Allspice liqueur
1⁄4 shot	Demerara/Muscovado/brown sugar syrup (2 sugar:1 water)
1⁄4 shot	Honey syrup (3 honey to 1 water)
3⁄4 shot	Pink grapefruit juice (freshly squeezed)
3⁄4 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 barspoon	Xanthan gum (E415) (optional)
review: With is trio of rums at a full measure a piece, this maritime sour is one of the punchiest on the classic roster of Tiki cocktails.
history: Created circa 1940 by Donn Beach at his Don the Beachcomber restaurant and subsequently reimagined by others, most notably Trader Vic. This version is closest to Trader Vic's recipe, but the ice-cone serve is a Donn Beach touch.

name: Tequila Fruit Cup (Difford's Cup No.7)
garnish: Lemon, orange & strawberry slices, mint sprig & borage
preparation: POUR all ingredients into glass. Half fill glass with ice. Add a citrus slice and a couple of mint leaves from garnish before filling to brim with ice. Finish with rest of garnish.
ingredients:
5⁄6 shot	Patrón Reposado tequila
5⁄6 shot	Orange Curaçao liqueur
5⁄6 shot	Strucchi Rosso Vermouth
2 dash	Bob's Lavender Bitters
1 2⁄3 shot	Thomas Henry Ginger Ale
1 2⁄3 shot	Cola (e.g. Coca Cola or Pepsi Cola)
review: Despite being in a relatively small proportion to all the other ingredients in this summery cocktail, tequila's distinctive notes shine through in the finished drink. We've used a reposado tequila but the drink works equally well, and slightly differently, with a blanco or añejo tequilas.
history: Created in June 2017 by yours truly at the Cabinet Room, London, England. For more recipes and history see Fruit Cups and Pimm's.

name: Frisco Sour
garnish: Lemon zest twist (discarded) & lemon slice wheel & maraschino cherry sail
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain back into shaker. DRY SHAKE (without ice) and fine strain into ice-filled glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Bourbon whiskey
1⁄2 shot	Bénédictine D.O.M. liqueur
1⁄2 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
1 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
1⁄2 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
review: A bourbon-laced sour with monastic herbal notes.
history:
The Frisco Sour started life as a mere Frisco, sans Sour (egg white) in Lucius-Beebe's 1946 The Stock Club Bar Book.
"Frisco Cocktail:
2 oz bourbon
¾ oz Benedictine
twist of lemon peel
Stir and serve in 3oz. cocktail glass."

The original Frisco is a tad sweet and is much improved with a dash or two of orange bitters to bolster the lemon oils from the twist. This obviously led a bartender somewhere to add citrus juice. In Stanley M. Jones 1977 Jones' Complete BarGuide he lists the above Frisco but with 2oz bourbon and ½oz Benedictine followed by a sour version:
"Frisco Sour
Sour glass Shake
½ oz lemon juice
¼ oz lime juice
¾ oz Benedictine
1-¼ oz whiskey
¼ tsp sugar
Lemon wedge, lime wheel"

Once this cocktail morphed into a sour then the addition of egg white was a natural progression, which I believe came in the 1990s when this was a popular cocktail in the London bar scene. That's when I first encountered the Frisco Sour which was by then served on-the-rocks. However, it also works well, as per Jones' recipe, strained into a stemmed sour glass or coupe.

name: Bourbon Crusta
garnish: Find a lemon which fits into a small wineglass tightly enough to act as a watertight extension to the glass. Cut off both ends of the fruit and carefully remove the pulp to leave a barrel-shaped shell of skin. Place in the top of the glass. Wet the edge of the glass and exposed fruit shell with sugar syrup and dip in caster sugar to frost the edge of both peel and glass. Leave for a couple of hours to form a hard crust.
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into pre-prepared glass.
ingredients:
2 shot	Bourbon whiskey
1⁄4 shot	De Kuyper Triple Sec (40%)
1⁄6 shot	Luxardo Maraschino liqueur
1⁄2 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
1⁄3 shot	Chilled water (omit if using wet ice)
review: Beautifully balanced bourbon and fresh lemon.
history: More Crusta cocktail information

name: Old Fashioned Cocktail (muddled fruit version)
garnish: Orange zest twist & Luxardo Maraschino cherry
preparation: MUDDLE orange and cherries in base of shaker. Add other ingredients, SHAKE with ice and fine strain into ice-filled glass.
ingredients:
2 whole	Maraschino cherry (from jar in syrup)
1⁄2 slice	Orange (fresh) (cut into segments)
1⁄2 slice	Lemon (fresh) (cut into segments)
2 1⁄2 shot	Bourbon whiskey
1⁄4 shot	Syrup from Luxardo Maraschino Cherries
1⁄4 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
review: This drink is often mixed in the glass in which it is to be served. Shaking better incorporates the flavours produced by muddling and fine straining removes the orange peel and cherry skin.
history:
Orange and lemon segments, and sometimes even a maraschino cherry, are sometimes muddled when making an Old Fashioned. The practise probably originated during Prohibition as a means of disguising rough spirits. This practice is almost unknown outside North America.

In the Foreword to his 1945 Cocktail Guide and Ladies' Companion, Lucus Beebe recants the reaction of a bartender at Chicago's Drake Hotel when ordering "an Old Fashioned without fruit except for lemon." "Yong impudent sir", he screamed, "my hair is hoary–with eld," he added as an afterthought. "Man and boy I've built Old Fashioned cocktails these sixty years. Yes, sir, since the first Armour was pushing a wheelbarrow in a slaughterhouse, and I have never yet had the perverted nastiness of mind to put fruit in an Old Fashioned."
Old-Fashioned cocktail history

name: The Ninth Ward
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Bourbon whiskey
1⁄2 shot	Elderflower liqueur
1⁄3 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄6 shot	Difford's Falernum liqueur
1⁄4 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 dash	Peychaud's or other Creole-style bitters
1⁄3 shot	Chilled water (omit if using wet ice)
review: Brother, forgive me, I've tweaked your cocktail in the quest for harmony between whiskey, elderflower, falernum, and lime. Ideally, I also add 5ml (1 spoon) bottled-in-bond rye whiskey. The Ninth Ward cocktail is also perhaps best served on-the-rocks rather than straight-up.
history:
Adapted from a recipe created in 2008 by Robert "Brother Cleve" Toomey in Boston, USA for Tales of the Cocktail. The cocktail is a play on the classic Ward Eight and a homage to one of the New Orleans neighbourhoods hardest hit by Hurricane Katrina. His original recipe comprised:
45ml (1½oz) Bourbon
22.5ml (¾oz) Lime juice
22.5ml (¾oz) Falernum
15ml (½oz) Elderflower liqueur
2 dash Peychaud's bitters

name: Rum Amandine
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Light white rum (charcoal-filtered 1-4 years old)
1⁄6 shot	La Fée Parisienne absinthe
1⁄6 shot	Luxardo Maraschino liqueur
1⁄2 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄3 shot	Giffard Orgeat Syrup
2 dash	Orange blossom water / Orange flower water
1⁄2 shot	Chilled water (omit if using wet ice)
review: A classic Daiquiri benefiting from the influence of maraschino, almond and absinthe.
history: Adapted from a recipe created by Marcis Dzelzainis at Quo Vadis in London, England.

name: French Maid
preparation: MUDDLE cucumber in base of shaker. Add next 5 ingredients, SHAKE with ice and fine strain into ice-filled glass. TOP with ginger beer.
ingredients:
3 slice	Cucumber (fresh)
8 fresh	Mint leaves
1 1⁄2 shot	Cognac (brandy)
1⁄2 shot	Difford's Falernum liqueur
3⁄4 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄3 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1 shot	Thomas Henry Ginger Beer
review: As Jim Meehan said when he gave us this recipe, "This hybrid of Audrey Saunders Gin Gin Mule substitutes cognac for gin and adds falernum and cucumber. Milk & Honey barman Sam Ross has a similar drink made with Bourbon dubbed the Kentucky Maid: consider this her spicy French sister."
history: Created in autumn 2007 by Jim Meehan at PDT, New York, USA for an art gallery opening hosted by John Pellaton of Hine Cognac.

name: Juliet & Romeo
garnish: Float 3 drops rose water, 3 drops Angostura bitters & mint leaf
preparation: MUDDLE cucumber with salt in base of shaker. Add other ingredients, SHAKE with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
3 slice	Cucumber (fresh)
1 pinch	Salt (sea salt)
8 fresh	Mint leaves
2 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
3⁄4 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄2 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: You smell rose water but taste gin, lime, cucumber and mint. A refreshing, summery cocktail.
history: Adapted from a recipe created circa 2007 by Toby Maloney at The Violet Hour in Chicago and featured in his 2022 book The Bartender's Manifesto.

name: Trader Vic's Sour
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain into ice-filled glass.
ingredients:
1 shot	Blended Scotch whisky
1⁄2 shot	Bourbon whiskey
1⁄2 shot	Cognac (brandy)
2⁄3 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄3 shot	Giffard Orgeat Syrup
1⁄6 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
3 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: Most sour renditions are strictly solo spirit-based, but why be so constricting when you can have a threesome? I like to let scotch have its way over the other two participants as this seems to help the trio sit harmoniously with the citrus and rich almond sugar. There's no need for block ice or other niceties – it's not that kind of trio.
history: Inspired by rather than actually made by Trader Vic. Indeed, this recipe is by Although you won't find a cocktail named a "Trader Vic's Sour" in any of his numerous books, he did like a sour with orgeat (e.g. his London Sour), and the proportions are in keeping with the essence of his numerous sour recipes.

name: Thirsty Monk
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Bourbon whiskey
1⁄2 shot	Bigallet Genepi Grand Tetras
1⁄2 shot	Bénédictine D.O.M. liqueur
1⁄2 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
3 dash	Peychaud's or other Creole-style bitters
3 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: A herbal bourbon-laced sour that's made special by dashes of creole bitters.
history: Created by Andrew King at FIG restaurant in Charleston, USA.

name: Mezcal Stone Sour
garnish: Orange juice and Classico Tajin Seasoning rim & orange zest twist
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain back into shaker. DRY SHAKE (without ice) to emulsify and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Del Maguey Vida Clásico mezcal
3⁄4 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
3⁄4 shot	Orange juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄2 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1⁄2 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
2 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
3 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: "Stone" in this mezcal sour refers to the inclusion of a splash of orange juice. It's delicious!

name: Between The Sheets
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
3⁄4 shot	Light white rum (charcoal-filtered 1-4 years old)
3⁄4 shot	Cognac (brandy)
3⁄4 shot	De Kuyper Triple Sec (40%)
1⁄4 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄12 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review:
The classic proportions for a Between the Sheets are most often quoted as being:
30ml (1oz) Light rum
30ml (1oz) Cognac brandy
30ml (1oz) Triple sec liqueur
7.5ml (¼oz) Lemon juice
That's three full shots of 40% liquor and a splash of lemon juice, which makes for a punchy cocktail that's just a touch on the tart side. My recipe uses a more manageable 67.5ml (2¼oz) of liquor (25% less) whilst broadly maintaining the classic proportions with just a touch of sugar (triple secs are drier these days) and saline to season.
history:
Between The Sheets probably originated as a gin and rum-based cocktail (during Prohibition) in America and then travelled to Europe where brandy was used in place of gin to make it more Sidecar-like. Although, this theory is upset by those who cite a Mr Polly of London's Berkeley Hotel as having created this cocktail in 1921.

Timeline: Between The Sheets first appeared in print in Frank Shay's 1929 Drawn From The Wood with a recipe that calls for gin rather than brandy.

name: Brandy Crusta
garnish: Some merely shove a wide long piece of lemon peel around the inside of the glass rim, leaving the drinker to push the peel down into the glass in order to sip from the drink. Instead I prefer the peel to become a watertight extension to the glass. Find a lemon which fits snugly in the top of a small wine, flute or sour glass. Cut off both ends of the fruit and carefully remove the pulp to leave a barrel-shaped shell of skin. Place in the top of the glass. Wet the edge of the glass and exposed fruit shell with sugar syrup and dip in caster sugar to frost the edge of both peel and glass. Leave for a couple of hours to form a hard crust that helps secure the peel.
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into pre-prepared glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Cognac (brandy)
1⁄4 shot	De Kuyper Triple Sec (40%)
1⁄4 shot	Luxardo Maraschino liqueur
1⁄2 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
review: This old classic zings with fresh lemon and is beautifully balanced by the cognac base.
history:
Created in the 1850s by Joseph Santini, an Italian from Trieste, in New Orleans, USA, either at the City Exchange in the French Quarter, or at his Jewel of the South saloon on Gravier Street in the American Quarter which he opened in 1855. The name refers to the crust of sugar around the rim.

Regarded by many as the forerunner to the Sidecar and, by extension, the Margarita, crusted sugar rim and all. The Brandy Crusta is a veritable member of cocktail royalty, so much so that it proudly takes its place as the fourth drink to be illustrated in the world's first cocktail book, Jerry Thomas' 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide where Santini is wrongly credited as being of Spanish origins and spelt Santana.

For more Crusta cocktail information see our page.

name: Champs-Elysees Cocktail
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Cognac (brandy)
1⁄3 shot	Green Chartreuse (or alternative herbal liqueur)
2⁄3 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄2 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
1⁄3 shot	Chilled water (omit if using wet ice)
review: A great after-dinner drink for lovers of cognac and Chartreuse.
history: A riff on the Sidecar, The Champs-Élysées is named after the touristy Parisian avenue. The first known recipe for this cocktail appears in Nina Toye and Arthur H. Adair's 1925 Drinks-Long and Short.

name: Saint-Marc Daiquiri
garnish: Lime slice or wedge on rim
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Light white rum (charcoal-filtered 1-4 years old)
1⁄2 shot	Bénédictine D.O.M. liqueur
3⁄4 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1⁄4 shot	Chilled water (omit if using wet ice)
1⁄24 shot	La Fée Parisienne absinthe
review: It's a Daiquiri with monastic Bénédictine and decadent absinthe influences-perhaps it's the saffron in the Bénédictine or the anise in the absinthe-but the result is truly a spiritual experience. It's simply divine.
history: Adapted from a drink discovered in 2014 at Bastille Cafe & Bar in Seattle, USA.

name: Eastside Gimlet
preparation: MUDDLE cucumber in base of shaker. Add gin, lime juice, sugar syrup and mint, SHAKE with ice and fine strain into chilled glass. TOP with a splash of soda.
ingredients:
2 slice	Cucumber (fresh)
8 fresh	Mint leaves
2 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
3⁄4 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄2 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1⁄2 shot	Thomas Henry Soda Water
review: A riff on the Southside and the Gimlet using cucumber, an ingredient inspired by Hendrick's Gin having recently launched when this gin cocktail was first created.
history: Created in 2004 by George Delgado at Libation, New York City, USA – originally as a long drink. Christy Pope took the Eastside to Milk & Honey where this now popular straight-up version was created.

name: Sidecar (Difford's spec.)
garnish: Orange zest twist (a lemon zest twist is more classic). There have been periods when it has been fashionable to coat the rim of the glass in which this cocktail is served with sugar. The earliest written reference to this is in 1934. Thankfully, sugar rims are now out of vogue, and, as Embury writes in his book, "A twist of lemon may be used if desired and the peel dropped into the glass. Otherwise no decoration."
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Cognac (brandy)
3⁄4 shot	De Kuyper Triple Sec (40%)
1⁄2 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄6 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1⁄4 shot	Chilled water (omit if using wet ice)
4 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review:
Cognac shines over freshening lemon and orange zestiness. Hopefully, you'll find this recipe perfectly balanced, but those with a sweet tooth may prefer to serve in a glass with a sugar rim - as has become traditional for a Sidecar.

For added complexity, replace the sugar syrup and chilled water in the recipe with 15ml (½oz) Pineau des Charentes blanc.
history:
The proportions of this cocktail are debated as much as the Sidecar's origin. Perhaps due to ease rather than balance, the equal parts formula (1 x brandy, 1 x triple sec and 1 x lemon juice) was the earliest published recipe (Robert Vermeire's 1922 Cocktails: How to Mix Them and Harry McElhone's 1922 ABC of Cocktails) and remains seems popular.

In his 1948 Fine Art of Mixing Drinks, David A. Embury writes of the 'equal parts' Sidecar, "This is the most perfect example of a magnificent drink gone wrong". He argues, "Essentially the Side Car is nothing but a Daiquiri with brandy in the place of rum and Cointreau in the place of sugar syrup or orgeat." Embury then gives his 8:2:1 Daiquiri formula (2 brandy, 1/2 triple sec and 1/4 lemon juice).

In his 1930 The Savoy Cocktail Book, Harry Craddock calls for 2 brandy, 1 Cointreau and 1 lemon juice.

Some refer to MacElhone and Vermiere's equal parts recipe as belonging to "the French school," while the Savoy's 2:1:1 formula is said to be from the "English school."

My recipe takes the middle ground between The Savoy and the 'equal parts' camp. I also find this cocktail benefits from a dash of sugar syrup, or (preferably) Pineau des Charentes, to help balance the citrus. If using just-out-the-freezer ice, also consider adding a splash of chilled water for dilution.

name: White Lady
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain back into shaker. DRY SHAKE (without ice) and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
3⁄4 shot	De Kuyper Triple Sec (40%)
3⁄4 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄6 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix) (optional)
3 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
1⁄2 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
review:
A simple, silky and delicious gin-laced classic with a sour finish.

My White Lady recipe is authentic to the proportions in Harry Craddock's 1930 recipe (see below) in using 2 parts dry gin, 1 part triple sec and 1 part lemon juice, but the sugar in modern-day triple secs (such as Cointreau) fails to balance lemon's citrus acidity (many triple sec liqueurs have become drier post-2000) so, depending on the sourness of your lemons, it is desirable to add a dash or even splash of sugar syrup.

Led by The Savoy's American Bar itself, where Peter Dorelli always made his signature White Lady with egg white, this addition has become the norm in most countries. However, while the Japanese enjoy raw fish, the trend for adding raw egg to sour cocktails is yet to catch on there, with Japanese bartenders such as Hidetsugo Ueno San vehemently against egg white being used in any cocktail.

I believe the Japanese omission of egg white is more a cultural judgement than one of taste, and egg white rounds a White Lady. It also makes it white. Beneath the attractive fluffy white foam produced by aerating the egg lies a dirty yellow drink that hardly befits the name. Those against the use of egg white argue that the drink is not named after its colour but the numerous ghostly white ladies of mythology. Maybe, but dirty yellow is not as visually appealing as a fluffy white head, and the drink's better with it!
history:
Like so many cocktails, the history of the White Lady is debatable. However, the recipe we recognise today originated in the late 1920s, probably created by Victor Cabrin at London's Grosvenor House Hotel, and was popularised by Harry Craddock, who included it in his 1930 The Savoy Cocktail Book.

Harry MacElhone, from Dundee, Scotland, created the first White Lady cocktail while working at London's Ciro's Club in 1919. However, this consisted of equal parts brandy, crème de menthe, and Cointreau, shaken and strained into a cocktail glass, so very different from the White Lady we know today with gin, triple sec, and lemon juice.

Harry's brandy-based crème de menthe recipe appears in his 1922 Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails and is repeated the following year as in Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails.

name: Honolulu Cocktail No. 1
garnish: Pineapple wedge with skewered Luxardo Maraschino Cherry
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
1⁄3 shot	Orange juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄3 shot	Pineapple juice
1⁄3 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄3 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: Gin is hardly Hawaiian, but its botanical bite sits well in this tropically fruity cocktail.
history: Adapted from a recipe in Harry Craddock's 1930 The Savoy Cocktail Book.

name: Beuser & Angus Special
preparation: SHAKE first 5 ingredients with ice and strain back into shaker. DRY SHAKE (without ice) to emulsify and fine strain into glass filled with crushed ice. FLOAT half a barspoon of orange flower water.
ingredients:
1 3⁄4 shot	Green Chartreuse (or alternative herbal liqueur)
1⁄3 shot	Luxardo Maraschino liqueur
1⁄2 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄2 barspoon	Powdered sugar (white sugar ground in mortar and pestle)
1⁄2 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
1⁄12 shot	Orange blossom water / Orange flower water
review: A floral, aromatic and herbal Chartreuse flip.
history: Adapted from a recipe created in 2007 by Gonçalo de Sousa Monteiro at Victoria Bar in Berlin, Germany. Gonçalo was inspired to make this cocktail for two fellow 'Travelling Mixologists', Bastian Heuser and Angus Winchester.

name: The Salty Bird
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain into ice-filled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Light white rum (charcoal-filtered 1-4 years old)
3⁄4 shot	Strucchi Red Bitter Liqueur
1 1⁄2 shot	Pineapple juice
1⁄2 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
8 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: Salty Bird hardly suggests a sweet fruity drink but perfectly befits this bittersweet rum-laced pineapple sipper.
history: Adapted from a recipe created by Lauren Schell at The Everleigh in Melbourne, Australia and promoted by Campari in 2013.

name: Smoky Whisky Sour
garnish: Lemon zest twist & Angostura bitters drawn across foam
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain back into shaker. DRY SHAKE (without ice) and strain into ice-filled glass.
ingredients:
1 shot	Caisteal Chamuis peated scotch whisky
1 shot	Blended Scotch whisky
1 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
3⁄4 shot	Maple syrup
1 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
1⁄2 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
review: Islay single malt and maple syrup add a distinctive smoky character to this otherwise classic Scotch Whisky Sour.
history: Created in November 2014 by yours truly at the Cabinet Room, London, England.

name: The French Canadian
preparation: MUDDLE cucumber in base of shaker. Add other ingredients, SHAKE with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 slice	Cucumber (fresh)
2⁄3 shot	Cognac (brandy)
1⁄2 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
1⁄3 shot	Maple syrup
1⁄2 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
review: Dry and aromatic with cucumber adding freshness. A good apéritif cocktail.
history: Created in 2015 by Dan Corum Fisher at Hawksmoor in Air Street, London, England.

name: Picasso Sour
garnish: Spray Angostura Bitters through stencil or drip a few drops on surface foam.
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain back into shaker. DRY SHAKE (without ice) and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	BarSol Mosto Verde Italia Pisco
1⁄2 shot	De Kuyper Triple Sec (40%)
5⁄6 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
2⁄3 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
1⁄3 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
4 dash	La Fée Parisienne absinthe
review:
We were struck by the photograph that accompanied the recipe sent to us by this cocktail's creator. The photo was of the cocktail at Burj Al Arab in Dubai, where it is served with a tiny wooden artist's colour palate alongside a micro easel holding a print of Picasso's Portrait of The Absinthe Drinker.

The cocktail itself is an artistic citrus-led riff on a Pisco Sour, but the original presentation amounts to true cocktail artistry.
history: Adapted from a recipe created in 2016 by Sean Halse at Gold On 27, Burj Al Arab, Dubai. Sean says, "The drink was designed to show the artistic side of the modern bartender." (His original recipe called for 40ml Lapostelle Pisco and 10ml 1:1 sugar syrup.)

name: Elixir Tropical
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
2 shot	Light white rum (charcoal-filtered 1-4 years old)
2⁄3 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
2⁄3 shot	Giffard Orgeat Syrup
1⁄4 shot	Luxardo Maraschino liqueur
3 dash	Angostura Aromatic Bitters
3 fresh	Mint leaves
review: There's a load of orgeat (almond syrup) in this Daiquiri-style cocktail, but it's only just on the sweet side of balanced with that almond richness contributing to its tropical character.
history: Created for Bacardí Legacy 2017 by Maurizio la Spina at Bartender's Italia, Naples, Italy.

name: Easy Street
garnish: Cucumber slice wheel speared with mint sprig bouquet
preparation: MUDDLE cucumber in base of shaker. Add next 4 ingredients, SHAKE with ice and strain into ice-filled glass whilst also pouring soda.
ingredients:
3 slice	Cucumber (fresh)
1 1⁄2 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
1⁄2 shot	Elderflower liqueur
1⁄2 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄6 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1 2⁄3 shot	Thomas Henry Soda Water
review: Gin-laced Cucumber and elderflower with a splash of freshening lemon juice and enlivened with soda. Perfect for a summer afternoon.
history: Adapted from a recipe created in 2010 by Anthony Schmidt at Noble Experiment in San Diego, USA.

name: Neptune's Wrath
garnish: Theatrically (but very carefully) pouring flaming Chartreuse is garnish enough!
preparation: SHAKE first 5 ingredients with ice and strain back into shaker. DRY SHAKE (without ice) to emulsify and fine strain into chilled glass. POUR Chartreuse into a long-handled metal measuring cup, ignite and then carefully pour flaming Chartreuse into cocktail.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
1⁄4 shot	La Fée Parisienne absinthe
3⁄4 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄2 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1⁄2 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
1⁄4 shot	Green Chartreuse (or alternative herbal liqueur)
review: Last Word-like with egg-white smoothing the way for a noticeable slug of absinthe.
history:
Adapted from a recipe created circa 2007 by Toby Maloney at The Violet Hour in Chicago, USA. The foaming surface, green hue of the absinthe and flaming Chartreuse represents Neptune expressing his fury with a dangerously rough sea.
Last Word history

name: Ranch Water
garnish: Lime slice wheel or lime wedge
preparation: POUR first 5 ingredients into glass and stir to combine. Fill glass with ice, top with soda/sparkling mineral water and briefly stir.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Patrón Silver blanco tequila
3⁄4 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄3 shot	De Kuyper Triple Sec (40%)
1⁄3 shot	Agave syrup
4 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
2 1⁄2 shot	Thomas Henry Soda Water
review: This refreshing Rickey-style cocktail is best made as per the original recipe, with a slightly salty sparkling mineral water such as Topo Chico. My recipe assumes suitable mineral water is not available so in an attempt to replicate Topo Chico, I have added a few drops of saline solution (or a pinch of sea salt) to soda water (club soda).
history:
Kevin Williamson is widely credited with creating this cocktail which has become something a staple across the state of Texas. He says the drink has been on the menu of his Ranch 616 Restaurant in Austin, Texas, USA since they opened in 1998.

The White Buffalo Bar at the Gage Hotel in Marathon, Texas is also associated with this cocktail's origin and Williamson says that it was his team who introduced the cocktail to Gage Hotel.

name: Smoke Show
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain back into shaker. DRY SHAKE (without ice) and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Del Maguey Vida Clásico mezcal
1⁄4 shot	Green Chartreuse (or alternative herbal liqueur)
1⁄4 shot	Cynar or other carciofo amaro
1⁄2 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄3 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1⁄2 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
review: Your choice of mezcal, the "smoke" element in this cocktail, will greatly impact its flavour. Select well and the result will be a deliciously herbal and delicately smoky sour.
history: Adapted from a recipe created in 2022 by Elizabeth "Liz" Martinez at The Purple Pig Restaurant in Chicago, USA.

name: Sauvignon Blanc Punch
garnish: Pink grapefruit or lemon slice wheel
preparation: SHAKE first 5 ingredients with ice and strain into ice-filled glass. TOP with soda.
ingredients:
3 shot	Sauvignon blanc wine
1⁄2 shot	Bittersweet orange-red aperitivo
1⁄2 shot	Pink grapefruit juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄2 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄3 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2⁄3 shot	Thomas Henry Soda Water
review: Grassy flavours from the sauvignon blanc, as well as the wine's acidity, add to the fresh zestyness of the citrus.
history: Adapted from a recipe created by Alex Day at Death & Co. in New York City, USA.

name: Between The Sheets No.1 (gin + rum + triple sec)
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
3⁄4 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
3⁄4 shot	Light white rum (charcoal-filtered 1-4 years old)
3⁄4 shot	De Kuyper Triple Sec (40%)
1⁄4 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄6 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: Light rum and gin freshened and invigorated with citrus. This is the bright, youthful warm-up act of the Between the Sheets trilogy.
history: The first known recipe for Between The Sheets cocktail appeared in Frank Shay's 1929 Drawn From Wood and this calls for equal parts gin, rum and triple sec. (Whereas the Between the Sheets No. 3, the version that has become the modern-day standard is with brandy in place of gin.)

name: Between The Sheets No.2 (brandy + gin + triple sec)
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
3⁄4 shot	Cognac (brandy)
3⁄4 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
3⁄4 shot	De Kuyper Triple Sec (40%)
1⁄4 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄12 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: It may be the Between the Sheets No.3 (with brandy and light rum) that's most identified with this suggestive cocktail's name but as with The Godfather films, it's the first and second Between the Sheets that are perhaps worthy most acclaim.
history:
In his 1939 The Gentleman's Companion (Volume II), the globetrotting drinks writer, Charles H. Baker, recounts an afternoon escaping "Arab-Jewish riots... in Christianity's own heart city." Baker found respite in the "almost Egyptian-looking sanctum" of the luxurious King David Hotel where he enjoyed a Between the Sheets made by a bartender named Weber and copied the recipe from his bar book.

Weber's Between the Sheets recipe calls for equal parts "cognac, Cointreau, dry gin and lemon juice," and Baker says, "Like the American Side Car, and other truly worthwhile cocktails this invention is totally sound, and is already quite famous throughout the Near East." Tellingly, at the back of his book, where he talks about ingredients, for Cointreau, he says, "it is one of the six favourite liqueurs of the world, but is indicated in several very important cocktails like between the sheets."

name: Churchillian
preparation: POUR absinthe into chilled glass, swirl to coat and set aside. STIR other ingredients with ice and strain into absinthe-rinsed glass (without ice).
ingredients:
1⁄24 shot	La Fée Parisienne absinthe
1 shot	Cognac (brandy)
1 shot	Blended Scotch whisky
1⁄4 shot	Cynar or other carciofo amaro
1⁄4 shot	Green Chartreuse (or alternative herbal liqueur)
1⁄4 shot	Luxardo Maraschino liqueur
review: I can imagine Winnie sipping one of these accompanied by a fat cigar. This Churchillian is as formidable as its namesake and you may prefer it tamed with a few ice cubes rather than served Sazerac-style, as its creator intended.
history: Adapted from a recipe created in 2021 by Jason E. Clapham at the St. Edward's MCR at Oxford, England. Jason says, "What would you serve Winston Churchill, who wasn't a fan of cocktails? This might just persuade him. He drank (diluted) Johnnie Walker all day, enjoyed cognac after supper, and disliked vermouth." Appropriately, Jason specifies Johnnie Walker Black Label scotch whisky in his recipe.

name: The Parasol
garnish: Thin line of aromatic bitters across foaming surface
preparation: DRY SHAKE all ingredients (without ice) to emulsify. SHAKE again with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 1⁄2 shot	Bittersweet orange-red aperitivo
1 shot	BarSol Mosto Verde Italia Pisco
1⁄2 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄3 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1⁄2 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
review: This aperitivo is on the quaffable sweet side of bittersweet/sweet 'n' sour with attractive pisco notes.
history: Adapted from a recipe created in 2005 by Francis Schott, thanks to a suggestion by bartender Liz Opacity at Catherine Lombardi restaurant in New Brunswick, New Jersey, USA. Originally with different proportions of pisco, specifically Barsol Quebranta. Discovered via Robert Simonson's The Mix.

name: White Dragon
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and strain back into shaker. DRY SHAKE (without ice) to emulsify and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Patrón Silver blanco tequila
3⁄4 shot	De Kuyper Triple Sec (40%)
3⁄4 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄6 shot	Agave syrup
3 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
1⁄2 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
review: A tequila-based White Lady.
history: Adapted from a recipe created by Jim Meehan, Portland, USA.

name: Gin Basil Sour
preparation: MUDDLE basil in base of shaker. Add other ingredients, SHAKE with ice and strain back into shaker. DRY SHAKE (without ice) to emulsify and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
12 fresh	Basil leaves
2 shot	Hayman's London Dry Gin
3⁄4 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄3 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
1⁄2 shot	Egg white (pasteurised) or Aquafaba (chickpea water) or 3 dashes Fee Brothers Fee Foam cocktail foamer
3 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: As the name suggests, a basil-flavoured gin sour. Yum.
history:
I'd love to claim credit for this silky riff on Jörg Meyer's contemporary classic Gin Basil Smash, but while the proportions are mine, I've merely reworked Jordan Ajmal's Gin Basil Sours which he added to Difford's Guide as a fellow Discerning Drinker in 2021. Many thanks, Jordan.

When I showed this Gin Basil Sour to Jörg, he reminded me that it's very close to Erik Lorincz's Green Park, created ten years earlier.

name: Improved Japanese Cocktail
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into chilled glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Cognac (brandy)
3⁄4 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
3⁄4 shot	Giffard Orgeat Syrup
1⁄3 shot	Chilled water (reduce if wet ice)
2 dash	Peychaud's or other Creole-style bitters
3 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: Lemon juice and bitters add a touch of creole sourness to this riff on the brandy-based classic Japanese Cocktail from Jerry Thomas's Bar Tenders Guide.
history: Adapted from a recipe created circa 2015 by Toby Cecchini at his Long Island Bar in Brooklyn, New York City.

name: Scotch Stone Sour
garnish: Skewered half orange slice wheel and Luxardo cherry (sail)
preparation: SHAKE all ingredients with ice and fine strain into ice-filled glass.
ingredients:
1 2⁄3 shot	Blended Scotch whisky
3⁄4 shot	Lemon juice (freshly squeezed)
3⁄4 shot	Orange juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄2 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
2 dash	Orange Bitters by Angostura
3 drop	Saline solution 4:1 (20g sea salt to 80g water)
review: A Scotch whisky-based sour with orange juice, and all the better for it.
history: Adapted from a recipe in Vincent Sardi Jr. & George Shea's 1988 Sardi's Bar Guide.

name: Bajito
preparation: Lightly MUDDLE mint and basil in glass just enough to bruise. Add rum, sugar and lime juice. Half fill glass with crushed ice and CHURN (stir) with bar spoon. Add more crushed ice and CHURN some more. Continue adding crushed ice and churning until glass is full.
ingredients:
6 fresh	Mint leaves
6 fresh	Basil leaves
2 shot	Light white rum (charcoal-filtered 1-4 years old)
1 shot	Lime juice (freshly squeezed)
1⁄4 shot	Sugar syrup 'rich' (2 sugar to 1 water, 65.0°Brix)
review: Basically a Mojito with basil as well as mint.
history: Discovered in 2004 at Excelsior Bar, Boston, USA.

name: Brandy Sour
garnish: Lemon zest twist (discarded) and garnish with a skewered lemon slice wheel and Luxardo Maraschino cherry sail
